utterances.text: The first midterm mail-in ballots are going out today in North Carolina ahead of November's general election. but a Trump administration plan to drastically reshape how the U.S. Postal Service handles these ballots is hanging in the balance. utterances.text: A decades-long dispute over control of the Falkland Islands is heating up again. Argentine President Javier Milei announced plans to sanction oil companies working near the Falkland Islands last night. He also reasserted Argentina's claim to the islands in the South Atlantic Ocean. Just one problem: the UK has controlled the territory since 1833. The two countries fought a war over it in the early 1980s. Milei also took aim at an oil field project off the coast of the Falklands and involving Israeli and British firms, he called it a, quote, "concrete and urgent danger" and accused the companies of moving towards oil extraction without Argentina's permission. Britain's foreign minister hit back today, saying the UK's commitment to the Falkland Islands was, quote, "unwavering" and that the islanders' right to self-determination is grounded in international law. The US has long avoided taking a position on who should control the islands while recognizing Britain's de facto rule. President Trump suggested earlier this week that Washington could reconsider that stance. College football is back in earnest this weekend with a full slate of games, but the most interesting matchup may be in court. The Southeastern Conference, the SEC, has sued LSU in federal court over what it alleges is a coordinated campaign to recruit professional athletes. It comes as another judge cleared the way yesterday for former New Orleans Saints defensive lineman Xavien Harris and former Cleveland Browns tight end Daquan Wright to leave the NFL and return to college under head coach Lane Kiffin at LSU. Several dozen athletes are attempting to take advantage of new NCAA rules allowing for 5 full years of competition. The SEC said it plans to appeal the ruling allowing the players to compete. Quote, "The SEC will continue to defend this standard, the principle of fair competition, and the conference's authority to govern competition among its member universities." LSU says it will carefully review the court's order and will work with the SEC and the NCAA as the matter moves forward.
